> **Key takeaways**
> - A full class is a signal. Read it first: which times fill, how fast, and who is waiting.
> - A waitlist shows real demand and offers the seat to the next family when one opens, without you chasing anyone.
> - Add a second session only when demand holds and you have the staff and space for it.
> - Keep the group size you teach best, and tell waiting families plainly where they stand.

## A full class is good news, and a decision

A lot of our posts for vendors are about the opposite problem: empty seats and quiet weeks. If that is you, start with [why kids' classes quietly stop getting bookings](/blog/why-kids-classes-stop-getting-bookings-keep-class-times-rolling).

A class that sells out brings its own questions. Squeeze in two more children? Open another time? Start a list? The wrong choice can turn a full class into a tired instructor and a group that no longer works. Here is how to decide calmly.

## Read the demand first

Before you change anything, look at what is actually happening.

- **Which times fill?** A Saturday morning class that sells out while a Wednesday afternoon class has room tells you about family schedules, not just your class.
- **How fast?** A class that fills within days of opening points to demand you are not meeting yet. One that fills slowly over a term may be just right.
- **Who is asking?** Note the ages families mention. If most are younger than your current group, the answer may be a new class, not more seats.
- **Steady or seasonal?** A class can fill once because of a school break or a burst of word of mouth. Watch it for a few weeks before you build around it.

Keep simple notes: when each session filled, how many families asked after that, and the ages they mentioned. A notebook page is enough.

## Use a waitlist well

A waitlist gives families a fair way to wait for a seat, and gives you a running count of the demand you cannot serve yet.

- **Turn it on before the class fills.** Families who find a full class with no list simply leave, and you never learn they were there.
- **Keep it a sensible length.** A long list for a class where seats rarely open only sets expectations you cannot meet. If it keeps growing, plan more sessions, not a longer line.
- **Be fair and predictable.** First come, first served is easy to explain. If you make exceptions, such as for siblings, decide them in advance and say so.
- **Read it every week.** A list you never look at is just a queue. A list you read is free market research.

## When to add a second session or a new time

A steady waitlist is the clearest sign you may need more room. Check three things first.

**The demand repeats.** One busy month is not enough. Look for a list that stays full for several weeks, or families asking about the same time again and again.

**The time works for families.** The best second session is often close to the first: the same day an hour later, or a nearby day at the same time. A slot that suits you but clashes with school pick-up will fill slowly.

**You can run it as well as the first.** A rushed or short-staffed second session can hurt the name the first one built. If you cannot run it well yet, wait.

Start with a short run of weeks rather than a full term, so you can test the new time without a big commitment.

## Check staff and space before you add seats

Adding a seat or two to a full class is tempting. Check your limits honestly first.

- **Staff.** Decide the ratio that fits your activity and your youngest age, and keep to it. If two more children push you past it, you need another adult, not another chair.
- **Space.** Count the room with mats, easels or equipment out, not as it looks empty. Think about movement, safety and a crowded pick-up.
- **Materials and time.** More children means more supplies, setup and clean-up. Back-to-back sessions also need time between them to reset the room.

## Keep the group size right

Your best group size is the one where every child gets attention. Overfilling chips away at exactly what made the class popular: children wait longer for a turn, the quiet ones get less help, and parents notice. If a class is full, let it be full. A clear limit tells families you take the experience seriously.

## Split by age or level

Sometimes a full class is really two classes in one. Demand gives you a chance to split it.

- **By age:** one session for younger children and one for older ones, each with activities that fit.
- **By level:** a beginner group and a next-step group, so new children are not lost and experienced ones are not bored.

Both groups usually get better, and families have a reason to stay as their child grows. Describe each group clearly so parents pick the right one.

## Tell waiting families clearly and kindly

Waiting is easier when people know where they stand. When a family asks about a full class:

- **Be honest about the wait.** If seats rarely open mid-term, say so. A kind, clear answer beats false hope.
- **Offer another option** if you have one: a different time, a new session or next term.
- **Thank them for their patience,** and keep your tone warm, not salesy. They already want to come.

## Plan next term from demand

Your waitlist and notes are your best guide for next term.

- **Add sessions where demand was steady,** not where it spiked once.
- **Rethink a time that never filled,** so the room serves the times families want.
- **Open the new schedule early,** so families who waited get a fair chance to book.
- **Keep the pattern steady.** Families plan around the same day and time each week.

## How ORYN Quest fits

Today ORYN Quest is open only in Southern California, and only approved vendors can list. A few tools help when a class fills up:

- **Total seats and a waitlist.** Both are optional details on a listing, along with age range and skill level. You turn the waitlist on per listing and set a maximum size (the default is 30).
- **A 24-hour hold.** When a seat opens, the next family gets a 24-hour hold. Unused holds pass to the next family, so you don't chase anyone.
- **What you see.** On the waitlist you see the parent's name, the child's first name and each family's place in line. You get no contact details.
- **A second session.** Add time slots one at a time, or a whole term at once from a repeating pattern (weekly, every 2 weeks, monthly).
- **Keep repeating.** For a weekly class, ORYN adds new class times automatically, so there are always about 8 weeks of sessions ahead to book. You can stop repeating at any time; existing bookings stay as they are.
- **Booking emails.** You get an email for every new booking, so you can watch a new session fill.

## FAQ

### Should I add more seats to a full kids' class?
Only if you stay within the ratio and space that let you teach well. If not, open a second session instead.

### How long should a kids' class waitlist be?
About as long as the seats that usually open in a term. A list that keeps growing is a sign to add a session.

### When should I add a second session?
When the waitlist stays full for several weeks, families keep asking about the same times, and you have the staff and space to run it well.

### What happens on ORYN Quest when a seat opens in a full class?
If the waitlist is on, the next family gets a 24-hour hold. Unused holds pass to the next family.
